title: Month 1: Linux Fundamentals
description: Month 1 of a nine month DevOps roadmap for complete beginners. Twenty six study days at three to six hours per day, six days per week. You will build a Linux virtual machine, live in the terminal, and deliberately break and fix things. Python and Bash practice runs as a separate daily course.

tasks.title: Install VirtualBox and create an Ubuntu Server 24.04 virtual machine with 2 CPUs and 4GB RAM.
Boot the VM, log in, and run whoami, hostname and date.
Read what a shell is and how it is different from a terminal window.
Run pwd, ls and clear. Say out loud what each one printed before moving on.
Use the up arrow and the history command to repeat commands you already ran.
Start a notes file. Write down every new command you learn this month with one line about it.
Practise cd with absolute paths like /var/log and relative paths like ../bin until both feel normal.
Learn what . and .. and ~ and / mean. Move between all four without looking anything up.
Run ls with -l, -a, -h and -R. Work out what every column in the long listing means.
Use tab completion for every single path you type today. Do not type a full path once.
Install tree and print the first two levels of the filesystem to see the shape of it.
Drill: from any random directory, get to /var/log in one command. Repeat ten times.
Create a nested folder structure with mkdir -p and put empty files in it with touch.
Copy and move files and folders with cp and mv. Learn why cp needs -r for directories.
Use wildcards to act on many files at once, for example rm *.log and cp report-*.txt backup/.
Learn why rm has no undo and no recycle bin. Read what rm -rf / does before you ever type it.
Break it: delete a file you still needed. Sit with the fact that it is gone forever.
Rebuild a five level folder tree from memory using only mkdir and touch.
Read a long file with cat, then with less. Learn to search inside less with slash and quit with q.
Use head and tail to look at the start and end of /var/log/syslog.
Run tail -f on a log file, then trigger new lines in another terminal and watch them appear.
Count lines, words and characters in a file with wc.
Edit a file with nano. Save it, close it, reopen it and confirm the change stuck.
Watch a short video on surviving vim, mainly how to quit it.
Read the man page for ls end to end. Find three flags you did not know about.
Learn what the numbered man sections mean and try man 5 passwd.
Compare the output of a tool with --help against its full man page.
Use apropos to find a command when you only know what it should do, not its name.
Install tldr and compare its examples to the official man page.
Challenge: solve three unfamiliar tasks today using only man and --help. No search engine.
Read an overview of the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard.
Explore /etc and open three config files in read only mode. Do not change anything yet.
Explore /var/log and identify which file records authentication attempts.
Compare /home and /root. Work out why root has its own home directory.
Find out what happens to files in /tmp when the machine reboots. Test it.
Look inside /usr/bin and /sbin. Explain to yourself why they are separate.
Use find with -name to locate every .conf file under /etc.
Combine find with -type and -size to list files over 10MB on the system.
Use find with -mtime to list files changed in the last two days.
Use find with -exec to run a command on every file it matches.
Use which and whereis to find where an installed program actually lives.
Challenge: find the five largest files in /var and write the command in your notes.
Search for a word inside a single file with grep.
Use grep with -i, -r, -n and -w. Know what each one changes.
Use grep -v to exclude lines and grep -c to count matches.
Search /var/log for failed login attempts and count how many there were.
Read a beginner introduction to regular expressions, covering only dot, star, caret and dollar.
Challenge: find every line in /etc that mentions ssh, ignoring case, showing line numbers.
Send command output into a file with the greater than sign. Confirm the file was overwritten.
Append output to a file instead of overwriting it, and prove the difference.
Learn the difference between stdout and stderr, then redirect only errors to a file.
Chain three commands together with pipes, for example ls, grep and wc.
Use tee to write output to a file and still see it on screen.
Send unwanted output to /dev/null and explain what /dev/null actually is.
Sort a file and remove duplicates with sort and uniq. Learn why uniq needs sorted input.
Pull a single column out of /etc/passwd using cut with a colon delimiter.
Use tr to change lowercase to uppercase and to delete characters.
Watch a short introduction to awk. Learn only how to print a chosen column.
Watch a short introduction to sed. Learn only how to replace text in a file.
Build one pipeline that finds the ten most common commands in your shell history.
Run whoami and id. Work out what the numbers next to your name mean.
Read /etc/passwd and explain every field on your own line.
Look at /etc/shadow and find out why a normal user cannot read it.
Create a new user called testuser, set a password, and log in as them.
Create a group, add testuser to it, and confirm with the groups command.
Switch between users with su and understand the difference between su and su dash.
Read how read, write and execute permissions work for owner, group and others.
Decode the permission string in ls -l for ten different files without help.
Set permissions using numeric mode. Know what 755, 644 and 600 mean by heart.
Set the same permissions again using symbolic mode with u, g, o and plus and minus.
Work out why a directory needs execute permission to be entered at all.
Break it: chmod 000 a file you need, watch it fail, then fix it.
Change the owner of a file with chown and confirm with ls -l.
Change the group of a file and set owner and group together in one chown command.
Run umask, then create a file and work out how umask decided its permissions.
Build a directory that two users can both write to, and test it with testuser.
Read what setuid, setgid and the sticky bit do. Look at the permissions on /tmp.
Fix a directory whose permissions you deliberately broke, without recreating it.
Run a command that fails as a normal user, then run it again with sudo.
Read why running everything as root is dangerous, even when it is convenient.
Find where sudo usage is logged and read your own entries from today.
Look at /etc/sudoers using visudo. Read it, change nothing.
Write three sentences in your notes explaining least privilege in your own words.
Give testuser sudo rights, test them, then take the rights away again.
Install and start the OpenSSH server on your VM.
Connect to the VM from your host machine using a password.
Generate an SSH key pair with ssh-keygen and look at both files it created.
Copy your public key to the server with ssh-copy-id and log in without a password.
Turn off password login in sshd_config, restart the service, and confirm keys still work.
Set up an entry in your local .ssh/config so you can connect by short name.
List running processes with ps aux and read what each column tells you.
Install htop and watch CPU and memory live while you load the machine.
Find a process ID and its parent process ID, and explain the relationship.
Stop a process with kill, then with kill -9. Learn why -9 is a last resort.
Read what SIGTERM, SIGKILL and SIGHUP mean and when each one is used.
Break it: start an infinite loop that eats CPU, find it in top, and kill it.
Run a long command in the background using an ampersand at the end.
Suspend a running command with Ctrl and Z, then check it with jobs.
Move a suspended job to the background with bg and back to the front with fg.
Start a process with nohup, close the terminal, and confirm it is still running.
Install tmux and learn only three things: new session, detach, and reattach.
Run three background jobs at once and manage all of them from one terminal.
Install nginx and confirm you can load its default page in a browser.
Read the full output of systemctl status nginx and understand every line.
Start, stop and restart nginx and watch the status change each time.
Enable nginx to start at boot, then reboot the VM and confirm it came back up.
Break it: put a syntax error in the nginx config, watch the restart fail, then fix it.
Read the nginx unit file and find out where systemd stores unit files.
Read system logs with journalctl and page through them properly.
Filter logs to a single service with journalctl -u nginx.
Follow logs live with journalctl -f while you restart a service in another terminal.
Filter logs by time using since and until.
Break nginx again, then find the exact error in the logs without asking anyone.
Read what logrotate does and why logs do not fill the disk forever.
Run apt update and apt upgrade, and understand the difference between them.
Install three tools you will use later: git, curl and tree.
Search for a package with apt search and read its details with apt show.
Remove a package with apt remove, then compare it to apt purge.
List installed packages with dpkg and find which package owns a specific file.
Read where apt gets its packages from by looking at the sources list.
Check free disk space with df -h and read every column.
Find which directory is using the most space with du and sort.
List block devices with lsblk and match them to what df shows.
Add a second virtual disk to the VM, format it, and mount it to a folder.
Read /etc/fstab and find out how mounts survive a reboot.
Break it: fill the disk with a large dummy file, watch things fail, then clean up.
Create a tar archive of a folder and check its size.
Extract a tar archive into a different location and verify the contents match.
Compress with gzip and compare the file size before and after.
Copy a file from your host machine to the VM using scp.
Sync a folder with rsync, then run it again and notice it only copies what changed.
Write down in plain English the steps of a nightly backup you could automate later.
Print all environment variables with env and pick out five you recognise.
Print your PATH and explain how the shell decides which program to run.
Create a variable, export it, and prove that a child process can see it.
Edit .bashrc, add something, and reload it with source.
Create three aliases that save you typing and make them permanent.
Break it: put a bad directory at the front of PATH, watch commands fail, then fix it.
Open your user crontab with crontab -e and look at the comments inside it.
Learn the five time fields and write out three schedules on paper before typing them.
Create a cron job that writes the date to a file every minute. Confirm it runs.
Find where cron logs its runs and read the entries from your test job.
Learn why cron jobs often fail because of PATH, then make one fail on purpose and fix it.
Write a cron job that deletes files in a folder older than seven days.
Create a script file, add a shebang line, and make it executable with chmod.
Use variables in a script and print them with echo. Learn when to use quotes.
Read arguments passed to your script using dollar one and dollar two.
Add an if statement that checks whether a file exists before acting on it.
Write a for loop that runs the same action on every file in a folder.
Write one useful script: back up a folder to a timestamped tar file.

days.title: Break It, Fix It, Write It Down

tasks.title: Take a VM snapshot so you can recover if today goes badly.
Have a friend break three things on your VM: a service, a permission and a config file.
Diagnose all three faults using only logs, systemctl and your own notes.
Fix all three without restoring the snapshot.
Write a short report on each fault: what broke, how you found it, how you fixed it.
Create a GitHub repo for this journey and push your notes and your backup script.
Review your command notes from all 26 days and mark anything you still cannot do from memory.

questions.prompt: Which command prints the directory you are currently in?
questions.explanation: pwd stands for print working directory and shows your current location.

questions.prompt: What does the ls -a flag do?
options: Shows file sizes in a readable form
questions.explanation: The -a flag shows all files, including hidden ones whose names start with a dot.

questions.prompt: What does the tilde character mean in a path?
questions.explanation: The tilde is a shortcut for the current user home directory.

questions.prompt: Which command copies a whole directory and everything inside it?
questions.explanation: Directories need the -r flag, which tells cp to work recursively.

questions.prompt: What happens to a file deleted with rm?
options: It moves to a trash folder
It is gone with no built in undo
It is archived for thirty days
It is renamed with a dot prefix
questions.explanation: There is no recycle bin on the Linux command line, so rm is permanent.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the last ten lines of a file?
questions.explanation: tail shows the end of a file, and head shows the beginning.

questions.prompt: What does tail -f do?
options: Follows the file and shows new lines as they arrive
questions.explanation: The -f flag follows a file live, which is how you watch logs while something runs.

questions.prompt: Which command counts the number of lines in a file?
questions.explanation: wc counts words, lines and characters, and -l limits it to lines.

questions.prompt: How do you leave the less pager?
questions.explanation: Pressing q quits less and returns you to the prompt.

questions.prompt: What does the .. path mean?
questions.explanation: Two dots refer to the directory one level above the current one.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the manual for a command?
questions.explanation: man opens the manual page for a command.

questions.prompt: What is apropos used for?
options: Running a command as another user
Finding a command by what it does
questions.explanation: apropos searches manual page descriptions, which helps when you know the task but not the command name.

questions.prompt: The terminal and the shell are exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: The terminal is the window you type into, and the shell is the program that reads and runs your commands.

questions.prompt: Tab completion can finish both command names and file paths.
questions.explanation: Tab completion works for commands, paths and often arguments too, and it prevents a lot of typing mistakes.

questions.prompt: The history command lets you see commands you ran earlier in the session.
questions.explanation: history prints your recent command list, and you can rerun entries from it.

questions.prompt: Which directory normally holds system wide configuration files?
questions.explanation: /etc is the standard location for configuration files on a Linux system.

questions.prompt: Where would you normally look for system log files?
questions.explanation: /var holds data that changes, and /var/log is where logs are written.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to files in /tmp after a reboot?
questions.explanation: /tmp is for temporary data and is commonly cleared on reboot.

questions.prompt: Which find option searches by file name?
questions.explanation: The -name option matches against the file name, and it accepts wildcards.

questions.prompt: What does find with -exec do?
options: Runs a command on each matching file
questions.explanation: The -exec option runs a command against every file that find matched.

questions.prompt: Which command tells you where an installed program lives?
questions.explanation: which searches your PATH and reports the program it would actually run.

questions.prompt: What does grep -i do?
questions.explanation: The -i flag makes the search case insensitive.

questions.prompt: What does grep -v do?
options: Shows lines that do not match
questions.explanation: The -v flag inverts the match and returns everything except the matching lines.

questions.prompt: Which symbol appends output to a file without erasing it?
questions.explanation: One greater than sign overwrites the file, and two append to it.

questions.prompt: What does a pipe do between two commands?
options: Runs them at the same time
Sends the output of the first into the second
Saves both outputs to a file
Runs the second only if the first fails
questions.explanation: A pipe connects the output of one command to the input of the next.

questions.prompt: What is /dev/null used for?
questions.explanation: /dev/null discards anything written to it, so it is used to silence output.

questions.prompt: Why does uniq usually need sort before it?
options: It only removes duplicates that sit next to each other
questions.explanation: uniq compares each line with the one before it, so duplicates must already be adjacent.

questions.prompt: Which command extracts a single column from a delimited file?
questions.explanation: cut pulls out fields based on a delimiter you choose.

questions.prompt: stdout and stderr are two separate output streams that can be redirected separately.
questions.explanation: Normal output and error output are separate, which is why you can send errors to one file and results to another.

questions.prompt: The tee command writes output to a file and also shows it on screen.
questions.explanation: tee splits output in two directions, which is useful when you want a log and live feedback at once.

questions.prompt: Which file stores basic user account information?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd holds account details such as username, user ID and home directory.

questions.prompt: Why can a normal user not read /etc/shadow?
options: It holds password hashes and is restricted
It does not exist on modern systems
It is stored on a separate disk
questions.explanation: The shadow file contains password hashes, so it is readable only by root.

questions.prompt: What does the permission value 755 mean?
options: Owner read and write, others nothing
Owner full control, group and others read and execute
questions.explanation: 7 gives the owner read, write and execute, and each 5 gives read and execute.

questions.prompt: Which numeric mode gives the owner read and write and nobody else anything?
questions.explanation: 6 is read plus write for the owner, and the two zeros remove all access for group and others.

questions.prompt: Why does a directory need execute permission?
options: To be entered and have its contents accessed
questions.explanation: On a directory the execute bit controls whether you can enter it and reach the files inside.

questions.prompt: Which command changes the owner of a file?
questions.explanation: chown changes ownership, and it can set the group at the same time.

questions.prompt: What does umask control?
options: The default permissions on newly created files
questions.explanation: umask removes permission bits from the defaults when a new file is created.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of running everything as root?
options: A single mistake can damage the whole system
questions.explanation: Root has no safety limits, so an error affects the entire machine rather than one account.

questions.prompt: Which command should you use to edit the sudoers file safely?
questions.explanation: visudo checks the syntax before saving, which prevents you from locking yourself out.

questions.prompt: What does ssh-keygen create?
options: A public and private key pair
questions.explanation: It generates two matching keys, and only the public one is copied to the server.

questions.prompt: Which key from your SSH pair goes on the remote server?
questions.explanation: The public key goes on the server, and the private key never leaves your machine.

questions.prompt: What does ssh-copy-id do?
options: Installs your public key on the remote server
questions.explanation: It appends your public key to the authorized keys file on the remote machine.

questions.prompt: The principle of least privilege means giving an account only the access it actually needs.
questions.explanation: Limiting access reduces how much damage a mistake or a compromised account can cause.

questions.prompt: chmod symbolic mode and chmod numeric mode can produce the same result.
questions.explanation: They are two ways of writing the same permission change, so 644 and the symbolic form can match.

questions.prompt: Disabling password login for SSH and using keys instead makes a server harder to attack.
questions.explanation: Keys cannot be guessed the way passwords can, which removes the most common brute force route in.

questions.prompt: Which command shows a live view of running processes?
questions.explanation: top updates continuously, and htop is a friendlier version of the same idea.

questions.prompt: What is a PID?
questions.explanation: Every running process gets a numeric process ID that you use to control it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?
options: kill asks the process to stop, kill -9 forces it
kill only works on your own processes
questions.explanation: Plain kill sends a polite termination signal, while -9 cannot be caught or ignored.

questions.prompt: Why is kill -9 a last resort?
options: The process cannot clean up before dying
questions.explanation: A forced kill gives no chance to save data or release resources properly.

questions.prompt: What does adding an ampersand to the end of a command do?
questions.explanation: The ampersand starts the command in the background and gives you your prompt back.

questions.prompt: What does nohup protect a process from?
options: Being stopped when the terminal closes
questions.explanation: nohup shields a process from the hangup signal sent when a terminal session ends.

questions.prompt: Which command starts a service immediately?
questions.explanation: start runs the service now, while enable only sets it to launch at boot.

questions.prompt: What does systemctl enable do?
options: Sets the service to start at boot
questions.explanation: enable creates the link that makes systemd start the service on every boot.

questions.prompt: Which command reads logs for one specific service?
questions.explanation: The -u flag filters the journal down to a single unit.

questions.prompt: What does journalctl -f do?
questions.explanation: The -f flag streams new log entries as they are written.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between apt update and apt upgrade?
options: update refreshes the package list, upgrade installs newer versions
update installs packages, upgrade removes them
update needs root, upgrade does not
questions.explanation: update only refreshes what is available, and upgrade actually installs the newer packages.

questions.prompt: What does apt purge do that apt remove does not?
questions.explanation: purge deletes the configuration files as well as the package itself.

questions.prompt: A service that is running right now will automatically start again after a reboot.
questions.explanation: Running and enabled are separate states, so a running service still needs to be enabled to survive a reboot.

questions.prompt: Logs are usually the fastest way to find out why a service failed to start.
questions.explanation: systemctl status and journalctl normally point straight at the error, which is faster than guessing.

questions.prompt: You can find which installed package a file belongs to using dpkg.
questions.explanation: dpkg can search its database and report the package that owns a given file.

questions.prompt: Which command shows free disk space in a readable format?
questions.explanation: df reports filesystem usage, and -h prints the sizes in human readable units.

questions.prompt: What does du measure?
options: Space used by files and directories
questions.explanation: du reports how much space specific files and folders are consuming.

questions.prompt: What is /etc/fstab used for?
questions.explanation: fstab tells the system which filesystems to mount automatically at startup.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a tar archive?
questions.explanation: The c flag creates an archive, while x extracts one.

questions.prompt: What advantage does rsync have over scp for repeated copies?
questions.explanation: rsync compares source and destination and sends only the differences.

questions.prompt: What does the PATH variable control?
options: Which directories the shell searches for commands
questions.explanation: The shell walks through the PATH directories in order to find the program you typed.

questions.prompt: How do you apply changes to .bashrc without opening a new terminal?
questions.explanation: source reruns the file in your current shell so the changes take effect immediately.

questions.prompt: How many time fields does a standard cron schedule have?
questions.explanation: Cron uses minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.

questions.prompt: Why do cron jobs often fail even when the command works in your terminal?
options: Cron has a very limited PATH and environment
questions.explanation: Cron starts with a minimal environment, so full paths are usually needed.

questions.prompt: What is a shebang line?
options: A comment at the end of a script
The first line that tells the system which interpreter to use
A way to import other scripts
questions.explanation: The shebang at the top of the file points to the interpreter that should run the script.

questions.prompt: What must you do before running a script directly by its filename?
questions.explanation: A script needs the execute permission before it can be run as a program.

questions.prompt: How do you read the first argument passed to a bash script?
questions.explanation: Dollar one holds the first argument, and dollar zero holds the script name itself.

questions.prompt: Filling a disk to one hundred percent can stop services from working correctly.
questions.explanation: Many programs need to write temporary files or logs, so a full disk causes failures across the system.

questions.prompt: An alias defined in the terminal disappears when you close it unless you save it in a config file.
questions.explanation: Aliases only last for the session unless they are added to a file such as .bashrc.

questions.prompt: Writing down what broke and how you fixed it is a normal part of professional operations work.
questions.explanation: Written incident notes are standard practice, and they are what turn one fix into a repeatable skill.
